The KMR uses a touch-sensitive six-point (6P) calibration procedure, which can establish the position of objects relative to the robot or the robot relative to a workbench. The calibration object is a 100 × 100 × 50 mm rectangular cube. The robot touches the cube at six locations: three points on one plane, two points on a perpendicular second plane, and one point on a third plane perpendicular to the first two. These contacts define the three coordinate planes; their intersection establishes the coordinate-frame origin and the planes’ normals define the axes. The recorded contact coordinates are used to solve the calibration equations, analytically via a pseudoinverse. The excerpt reports testing with 100 separate calibrations while varying the initial position estimate by up to ±15 mm in x and y and ±2.5° in orientation. context: The study found that automated robot synthesis produced silica nanoparticles with greater accuracy and reproducibility than manual human synthesis. Robot-produced batches were monodisperse and showed consistent size distributions, whereas manual results varied with operator qualification and with differences in the timing and speed of steps such as tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) addition. The robot’s consistent execution reduced variation in nanoparticle size and distribution. Although the automated process took approximately 80 minutes longer in total because the robot and connected equipment required additional lead time, it substantially reduced hands-on labor. Manual personnel time ranged from 34 to 66 minutes, while automated synthesis required about 22 minutes on average, with a maximum of 30 minutes for preparation and refilling; the excerpt characterizes this as approximately 44% less human time. Personnel costs were estimated to decrease by 75% per synthesis. The platform used a dual-arm robot-based infrastructure with standard laboratory equipment and modular components, but the specific robot model or manufacturer is not identified in this excerpt. The system was described as flexible, programmable, repeatable, and suitable for wet-chemical nanoparticle syntheses involving mixing, centrifugation, and ultrasonication.
